title: Refining of Metals
notes: **Purpose of refining:** Crude metals obtained from smelting or electrolysing ores contain impurities (other metals, metalloids, non-metals) that degrade their properties. Refining removes these impurities to achieve the purity required for specific applications. Purity requirements vary: commercial copper is 99% pure, electrical-grade copper needs 99.99% (4N), and semiconductor-grade silicon requires 99.9999999% (9N).

**Poling:** A refining method for metals whose oxides are easily reduced by hydrocarbon gases. Molten impure metal is stirred with a green wooden pole (the 'pole'). The wood releases hydrocarbon gases (CH₄, CO, H₂) that reduce metal oxides to the pure metal: Cu₂O + CH₄ → 2Cu + CO + 2H₂. The process is named 'poling' because of the wooden pole used. Primarily used for copper (99.5% pure 'blister copper' is refined to 99.99% pure cathode copper). The gas bubbles also help remove dissolved gases (SO₂, O₂) from the melt.

**Electro-refining (electrolytic refining):** The most widely used refining method. The impure metal is made the anode, a thin strip of pure metal is the cathode, and a solution of the metal's salt serves as the electrolyte. On passing current: (1) Anode (impure): M → Mⁿ⁺ + ne⁻ (metal dissolves), (2) Cathode (pure): Mⁿ⁺ + ne⁻ → M (pure metal deposits), (3) Impurities: More electropositive impurities (Fe, Zn, Ni) dissolve into solution; less electropositive impurities (Ag, Au, Pt) fall to the bottom as 'anode mud' or 'anode slime'. This is how precious metals are recovered as by-products.

**Copper electro-refining setup:** Anode: impure copper castings (contains Fe, Zn, Ni, Ag, Au, Pt, Se, Te). Cathode: thin sheets of pure copper (99.99%). Electrolyte: acidified copper sulphate (CuSO₄ + H₂SO₄). Current density: 200–300 A/m². Voltage: 0.2–0.4 V. Duration: 24–48 hours. The anode loses ~1–2 mm per day. Anode mud contains Ag, Au, Pt, Se, Te — these are processed separately and are economically significant (the value of precious metals in anode mud can offset refining costs).

**Electro-refining equations for copper:** At anode: Cu(s) → Cu²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ (main reaction); Fe(s) → Fe²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻; Zn(s) → Zn²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻. At cathode: Cu²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ → Cu(s) (pure copper deposits). The Fe²⁺ and Zn²⁺ accumulate in the electrolyte but do not deposit because their reduction potentials are more negative than copper's. Periodically, the electrolyte must be purified to remove accumulated Fe²⁺ and Zn²⁺.

**Hoopes process (aluminium refining):** A three-layer electrolytic cell for producing 99.99% pure aluminium. Bottom layer: molten pure aluminium (cathode). Middle layer: molten electrolyte (Na₃AlF₆ + CaF₂ + AlF₃). Top layer: molten impure aluminium (anode). The pure aluminium collects at the bottom, protected from the electrolyte by the less dense impure aluminium on top. Carbon electrodes are used. This produces aluminium of 99.99% purity, suitable for electrical conductors and aerospace applications.

**Zone refining (zone melting):** Used for ultra-high purity metals (semiconductor grade). A narrow molten zone is passed repeatedly along a solid metal rod. Impurities are more soluble in the molten state than in the solid, so they concentrate in the molten zone and are swept to one end of the rod. After many passes, the majority of the rod is extremely pure. This is how silicon for semiconductors is purified to 9N (99.9999999%) — impurity levels below 1 part per billion.

**Vaporophonic refining (Mond process):** Used for refining nickel. Impure nickel is reacted with CO at 50–60°C to form volatile nickel carbonyl: Ni(s) + 4CO(g) → Ni(CO)₄(g). The gas is then heated to 200–250°C, where it decomposes: Ni(CO)₄(g) → Ni(s) + 4CO(g). Pure nickel deposits, and CO is recycled. This process produces nickel of 99.99% purity. The same principle applies to iron (iron pentacarbonyl Fe(CO)₅).

**Distillation refining:** Used for metals with low boiling points — zinc (bp = 907°C) and cadmium (bp = 767°C). The crude metal is melted and distilled; the vapour is condensed to give pure metal. Impurities with higher boiling points (Fe, Pb) remain in the residue. This is simple, energy-efficient, and produces very pure metal. Tin (bp = 2320°C) is also refined by distillation, though its high boiling point makes this energy-intensive.

**Chlorination refining:** Used for titanium and zirconium. Impure metal is converted to a volatile chloride (Ti + 2Cl₂ → TiCl₄), which is purified by fractional distillation, then reduced with magnesium or sodium: TiCl₄ + 2Mg → Ti + 2MgCl₂. This is the Kroll process, the dominant method for titanium production. The resulting titanium is 99.5% pure; further refining (electron beam melting) removes residual oxygen and nitrogen.

**Anode mud — economic significance:** During copper electro-refining, approximately 1–2 kg of anode mud is produced per tonne of copper. This mud contains silver (~300 g/tonne), gold (~5 g/tonne), platinum group metals, selenium, and tellurium. The value of these precious metals often exceeds the profit from the copper itself, making anode mud processing an integral part of copper refining economics.

**Purity requirements by application:** (1) Electrical copper: 99.99% (4N) — higher impurities increase electrical resistivity. (2) Aluminium for wiring: 99.8% — small amounts of Si and Fe are tolerable. (3) Silicon for semiconductors: 99.9999999% (9N) — even one impurity atom per billion can destroy device function. (4) Gold for electronics: 99.999% (5N) — surface contamination causes contact resistance. (5) Iron for steel: 99.5% — carbon and other elements are intentionally added.

**Comparison of refining methods:** (1) Poling — simple, low cost, specific to Cu/Ag; (2) Electro-refining — versatile, high purity, but energy-intensive; (3) Zone refining — highest purity, slow, expensive; (4) Mond process — elegant for Ni/Fe, but CO is toxic; (5) Distillation — simple for low bp metals; (6) Chlorination — essential for Ti/Zr, complex equipment needed. The choice depends on the metal, required purity, and economic factors.

**Historical context — electrolytic refining invention:** Michael Faraday demonstrated electrolytic metal deposition in 1834, but industrial electro-refining of copper was not implemented until 1887 by Emil WohlWill in Germany, who achieved 99.99% pure gold. The copper electro-refining process was developed independently by Charles Martin Hall (USA) and others. This innovation transformed copper from a structural material into an electrical conductor, enabling the electrification of the world.
confusion: Poling vs. Electro-refining: Poling uses a wooden pole to generate reducing gases that remove oxide impurities from molten metal — it is a chemical reduction process, not an electrochemical one. Electro-refining uses electric current to dissolve impure metal at the anode and deposit pure metal at the cathode — it is an electrochemical process. Poling is simpler and cheaper but only works for specific metals (Cu, Ag); electro-refining is universal.

Anode mud vs. Slag: Anode mud is the residue that falls from the ANODE during electro-refining — it contains precious metals (Ag, Au, Pt) and is economically valuable. Slag is the fusible waste product formed during SMELTING (ore processing) — it is a silicate mixture (CaSiO₃) that floats on molten metal and is discarded or used in cement. They come from completely different processes.

Zone refining moves the impurities, not the pure metal: In zone refining, the molten zone travels along the rod, carrying impurities with it. After many passes, the impurities concentrate at one END of the rod, which is then cut off. The rest of the rod becomes progressively purer. This is different from distillation, where the pure metal vapourizes and is collected separately.

Hoopes process layer order: The three layers in the Hoopes cell are: TOP (least dense) = molten impure Al (anode), MIDDLE = molten electrolyte (Na₃AlF₆-CaF₂-AlF₃), BOTTOM (most dense) = molten pure Al (cathode). The density ordering is critical: pure Al (2.02 g/cm³) sinks below the electrolyte (~2.1 g/cm³) but the impure Al anode must float above the electrolyte. The density differences are small (~0.1 g/cm³), so precise temperature control is essential.

Refining vs. Extraction: Refining purifies an ALREADY-EXTRACTED metal; extraction produces the metal from its ORE. Smelting (ore → crude metal) is extraction; electro-refining (crude metal → pure metal) is refining. The distinction matters because refining typically starts with a material that is already ~95–99% metal, while extraction starts with ore that may be only 1–5% metal.
practice: In copper electro-refining, an anode containing 98% Cu, 1% Fe, 0.5% Zn, 0.3% Ag, and 0.2% Au is used. Calculate the mass of pure copper deposited at the cathode when a current of 500 A is passed for 24 hours. Also determine which impurities dissolve in the electrolyte and which form anode mud. (Use Faraday's law: m = MIt/nF, where M(Cu) = 63.5 g/mol, F = 96500 C/mol.)

Describe the Mond process for nickel refining with balanced equations. Explain why this process is suitable for nickel but not for iron (iron carbonyl is less stable). Calculate the volume of CO gas required at STP to convert 100 kg of impure nickel (90% Ni) to Ni(CO)₄. (Ni + 4CO → Ni(CO)₄; molar mass Ni = 58.7 g/mol.)

Zone refining is used to purify silicon for semiconductors. If the distribution coefficient k = C_s/C_l = 0.1 for phosphorus in silicon (meaning P prefers the liquid phase), calculate the impurity concentration in the solid after one pass, assuming the initial concentration is 100 ppm. Use the Pfann equation: C_s = kC_0(1−x)^(k−1), where x is the fraction melted.

Compare the Hoopes process and the Hall-Héroult process for aluminium. Why can't the Hall-Héroult process directly produce 99.99% pure aluminium? Describe the three-layer cell design of the Hoopes process and explain why each layer has its specific position based on density.

A gold electro-refining cell operates at 0.3 V and 100 A for 12 hours. The anode contains 95% Au, 3% Ag, and 2% Cu. Calculate: (1) mass of pure gold deposited, (2) mass of anode mud (assuming Ag and Cu form the mud), (3) energy consumed in kWh. Discuss the economic significance of recovering silver and copper from the anode mud.
universalFacts: The WohlWill process (1874) produces gold of 99.999% purity (5N) — the standard for modern electronics. A single gold coin from ancient Rome, when refined by modern electro-refining methods, would yield a gold bar pure enough to be used in a microchip. The difference between 'pure' gold (24K, 99.5%) and 'electronic grade' gold (5N) is the difference between a wedding ring and a functioning CPU.

Michael Faraday's laws of electrolysis (1834) are the foundation of all electro-refining. His first law states that the mass of substance deposited at an electrode is directly proportional to the charge passed: m = Qt/F × (M/z). This means refining time is directly proportional to the amount of metal to be purified — a 1-tonne copper anode requires approximately 3000 kWh of electricity to refine completely.

The anode mud from copper refining contains more silver and gold per tonne than many silver and gold ores. A typical copper anode mud yields ~300 g Ag and ~5 g Au per tonne of copper. Some copper refineries are more profitable from precious metal recovery than from copper sales, making the economic balance of the entire operation highly sensitive to precious metal prices.

Zone refining was developed by American scientist William Pfann in 1952 at Bell Labs. It was the first method to produce semiconductors pure enough for the transistor revolution. Pfann showed that a single pass of a molten zone could reduce impurity levels by a factor of 10 or more. Today, zone refining is used to purify germanium, silicon, gallium arsenide, and many other semiconductor materials.

The Mond process for nickel was invented by German chemist Ludwig Mond in 1890. It was the first industrial process to produce a metal of 99.99% purity. The process is so elegant that it is still used today — over 70% of the world's nickel is refined by the carbonyl process. The toxic gas Ni(CO)₄ has an LD₅₀ of ~7 ppm in rats, making it one of the most toxic substances handled in industrial chemistry.
